title: Why Average Alone Is Not Enough

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A measure of central tendency, however well chosen, can hide very different underlying realities. A measure of dispersion reports how far the values lie from one another or from their centre.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Two clinics both report a mean waiting time of 20 minutes. In Clinic X almost everyone waits close to 20 minutes. In Clinic Y half the patients wait 5 minutes and half wait 35. The mean cannot tell the clinics apart, yet their problems, and the fixes they need, are completely different.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Clinic X’s waits: 18, 19, 21, 22 minutes (mean 20; range 4 minutes). Clinic Y’s waits: 5, 5, 35, 35 minutes (mean 20; range 30 minutes). Clinic Y probably has a subset of patients held up at one bottleneck, such as a particular test or specialist; Clinic X has a modest delay that affects everyone.

points.html: Identical central tendency can describe very different situations. Dispersion measures tell them apart.
Report a centre with a spread: mean with SD (§3.7), or median with IQR (§3.4). A mean reported alone hides exactly the difference between Clinic X and Clinic Y.
